name: Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa)
short: Deaths in US poison-centre and forensic reports (most with other substances); liver injury, 4 needing transplant, in case reports; dependence and withdrawal in a survey of regular users.
text: The evidence on harm comes from poison-centre data, forensic reports, case reports and surveys, not from controlled trials. Among 1807 kratom exposures reported to US poison control centres from 2011 to 2017, 31.8% of exposures in which kratom was the first-ranked substance led to admission to a health care facility and 51.9% to a serious medical outcome; there were 11 deaths, two of them after exposure to kratom only, and seven exposures in newborns, five with withdrawal; exposures involving several substances had greater odds of admission and of a serious outcome than kratom alone, and among kratom-only exposures the commonest effects were agitation or irritability and a fast heart rate. A forensic review of toxicology reports from 35 deaths in Northern Nevada (2015 to 2020) found mitragynine, the main kratom alkaloid, as the sole intoxicant in one case; blood levels did not differ significantly between deaths in which mitragynine was or was not listed as contributing. A 2026 systematic review of 31 studies, mostly single-patient case reports, described 32 cases of kratom-associated liver injury, mostly cholestatic with jaundice; most improved after kratom was stopped, but 4 progressed to liver transplantation, and polysubstance use was frequent. In a survey of 293 regular users in Malaysia, more than half had severe and 45% moderate kratom dependence, with withdrawal symptoms such as muscle spasms and pain, sleeping difficulty and diarrhoea. Seizures are among the most commonly reported side effects, but a 2025 systematic review of case reports, case series and adverse-event databases (20 patients in published reports; only one was quantitatively positive for mitragynine in urine, and the authors report no indication that the other 19 were screened, so they say there was minimal proof of kratom use) concluded that there is insufficient evidence to suggest that kratom causes seizures, mainly because toxicology reports gave no quantitative dose-response, medical records were incomplete and seizures occur relatively frequently in the general population. The cited sources name no specific medicine interactions; the poison-centre authors warn of the dangers of using kratom in combination with other substances.
